Worrell, E., Galitsky, C., Masanet, E. and Graus, W. (2008). Energy Efficiency Improvement and Cost Saving Opportunities for the Glass Industry: An ENERGY STAR Guide for Energy and Plant Managers. Report LBNL-57335-Revision, Ernest Orlando Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, Berkeley, CA, March 2008. No DOI or URL printed.

Locators are printed page numbers (PDF page = printed + 8). An ENERGY STAR measure catalogue; nearly every number is reprinted from other works (named in each note). Main file (27 technologies, 44 examples): Table 7 melting-furnace specific energy by segment (flat, container, specialty, insulation fiberglass, textile fibres) and furnace type (regenerative, oxy-fuel, electric boost, electric melter, direct melter, recuperative), natural gas and electricity as final energy with the printed average as value and printed range as min/max, converted from MMBtu per short ton with an explicit formula; electric melter state of the art (780-800 kWh/short ton), German survey (1.18 kWh/kg) and maximum capacity; plant examples with metric values: Heye Obernkirchen oxy-fuel (3.35 GJ/t), Gerresheim (old regenerative 5.028, oxy-fuel 3.436, oxy-fuel with batch/cullet preheat 3.017 GJ/t), tall-crown oxy-fuel, Vetropack Straza end-fired regenerative (4.0 GJ/t, 150 t/d), Sorg LoNOx melter (3.234 GJ/t), PPG P-10 segmented melter, submerged combustion (capacity, state); Table 9 post-forming (lehr, gas and electric tempering, laminating, autoclave, wool curing, textile fibres); Table 8 forming electricity; batch preparation electricity by segment; GlassMax cullet grinding (electricity, opex). _measures.csv: quantified measures of Sect. 5.1-5.11 as printed. _other-values.csv: Table 7 production shares and primary energy, Table 6 process-step averages, Rue et al. segment melting intensities, furnace physics (theoretical minimum, losses, efficiencies, campaign lives), oxygen production energy (denominator ambiguous), capacities and sector statistics. No flows. Not loaded: Tables 4-5 by fuel and year beyond totals, figures (charts only), qualitative measures, appendices. No emissions figures for any technology. Heating-value basis is never stated.

(1) Table 7 container-glass shares sum to 115% (70+15+30); electric melter n.a. (2) Table 7 italics (footnote 13: gas-only estimates) cannot be read from the text layer; specialty and fiberglass rows have no electricity column, assumed gas-only. (3) Gerresheim oxy-fuel with preheating printed 3.02 MJ/kg = 2.9 MMBtu/ton (p.65) and 3,017 kJ/kg = 2.6 MMBtu/ton (p.68); 3,436 kJ/kg = 3.0 and 419 kcal/kg = 0.36 MMBtu/ton (kcal should be kJ). (4) p.10 says about 90% of furnaces in each sub-sector are recuperative, contradicting p.63 (90% of glass melted in regenerative furnaces) and Table 7. (5) Specialty electric melter 10.3 MMBtu/ton (about 3,000 kWh/short ton) is 3-4 times the 780-800 kWh/ton state of the art. (6) Oxygen-production energy (p.64) printed per ton without saying whether ton of oxygen or of glass. (7) German survey 1.18 kWh/kg restated as 1070 kWh/short ton (exact 1070.5, fine). (8) Corning Greenville electricity saving printed as 9 MWh/year against 12,000 MMBtu gas added - probably 9 GWh. (9) Mixer consumption printed in kW/tonne. (10) No price year for most costs; GlassMax opex loaded with publication year 2008. (11) Duplicated paragraph on refining (p.10 and p.11).
